text: Today we're talking about 11 spices that
can lower blood pressure naturally. If
you want to bring your numbers down
without adding another medication, you
need to pay attention to something that
most people overlook. What you season
your food with. But here's the problem.
Most people think lowering blood
pressure means cutting out salt
completely, eating bland, boring food,
or following a miserable heart-healthy
diet. But here's the surprising truth.
Some of the most powerful blood pressure
supporting compounds in nutrition are
found in spices. And if used regularly,
the right spices can help blood vessels
relax, improve blood flow, and support
healthier blood pressure over time,
especially after the age of 60. By the
way, I'm Dr. Mitch Rice, a practicing,
board-certified primary care physician
here in the United States, and I want to
walk you through each of these 11 spices
by showing how they lower blood
pressure, what they do inside your body,
and how to use each of them without
changing your whole diet. By the way,
food always comes first. But if you
don't enjoy the taste of some of these
spices, but still want the added
benefits, I've linked a few simple
capsule options on Amazon below that are
a good backup, and you can check them
out in the description. The first spice
that we're talking about today is
garlic. Garlic contains a compound
called allicin. Allicin helps blood
vessels relax and widen. When blood
vessels open up, blood flows more
easily, the pressure inside the vessels
go down, and the heart does not have to
work as hard. Garlic is very strong. It
works almost like medicine. The best way
to use it is to put fresh garlic or
garlic powder in with cooking. Small
amounts used daily work best than larger
amounts once or twice a week. Spice
number two is cinnamon, and cinnamon
comes from tree bark. It smells warm and
tastes slightly sweet. Most of us have
had cinnamon before. Cinnamon actually
helps to control blood sugar, which is
essential for blood pressure. When blood
sugar rises too fast, stress hormones go
up, blood vessels tighten, and blood
pressure rises. Cinnamon helps slow this
down. It allows blood vessels to stay
more relaxed after meals. The best way
to use it is to sprinkle it on some
oatmeal, some apples, or yogurt. Spice
number three on our list is turmeric.
Turmeric is bright yellow, and it
contains a natural compound called
curcumin. Curcumin can help lower
swelling inside of blood vessels. Stiff
blood vessels raise blood pressure, and
turmeric helps blood vessels stay
flexible and calm. The best way to use
it is to use about half teaspoon in
soups, eggs, vegetables, or with warm
tea. A quick notice to always add black
pepper with the turmeric, as black
pepper helps your body absorb the
turmeric better. Spice number four is
ginger. And ginger is important because
it helps the blood flow more smoothly
throughout the body. It also can help
slightly relax the muscles around the
blood vessels. When those muscles relax,
blood flows easier, pressure drops, and
the heart does not have to work as hard.
Ginger also helps digestion, and better
digestion can support better blood
pressure control. The best way to use it
is fresh ginger either in tea or soup.
Ground ginger works just as well. The
fifth spice on this list is black
pepper. Black pepper contains a compound
called piperine or piperin. Piperin
helps protect blood vessels from damage,
improve how the body absorbs nutrients,
and it can help turmeric and other
spices work better. Black pepper may
seem simple, but it plays a big support
role. The best way to use it is to just
use a small amount every day with meals.
Spice number six is cardamom. Cardamom
is a warm spice with a light sweet
taste. It's often used in Indian and
Middle Eastern foods and it is full of
antioxidants. Antioxidants protect the
inside lining of blood vessels. When
blood vessels are healthy and relaxed,
the blood moves more easily and the
pressure inside the vessels go down.
Cardamom also helps the body release
extra water. Less fluid in the body
means less pressure. The best way to use
it again is to add a small pinch to tea,
rice, oatmeal, or some baked foods.
Spice number seven on our list is
cayenne pepper. Cayenne pepper contains
capsaicin. Capsaicin actually helps the
body make more nitric oxide. Nitric
oxide tells blood vessels to open and
relax. This helps blood move more freely
and lowers blood pressure. You don't
need spicy food for this to work. A
small amount used often is enough. The
best way that I found to use this is to
add a small pinch to eggs, soup, or over
some beans. Just like cayenne pepper,
spice number eight, oregano, is also
full of antioxidants. These protect the
blood vessels from getting damaged,
especially the inside walls of arteries.
Damaged blood vessels become stiff and
narrow and this can raise blood pressure
over time. Oregano also contains fiber
and fiber helps lower the bad
cholesterol. Lower cholesterol helps
blood flow better. Oregano is a widely
used spice, but I find it works best
when added to soups, vegetables, or
mixed together with olive oil used to
bake something. Spice number nine on our
list is thyme. Thyme helps lower a
substance in the body called ACE. ACE
can cause blood vessels to tighten. When
ACE levels are lower, blood vessels stay
more relaxed. Thyme can also help lower
cholesterol and both effects support
healthier blood pressure. The best way
to use it is to add time to things like
chicken, fish, or soups. Spice number 10
on our list is basil. Basil contains a
compound called eugenol. Eugenol helps
block too much calcium from entering
blood vessels. Too much calcium makes
blood vessels squeeze tight, and
blocking it helps blood vessels relax.
Just like we've seen before, when blood
vessels relax, this makes blood flow
easier. The best ways to use dried basil
on salads, eggs, or in sauces. Spice 11
on our list is nutmeg. And nutmeg is
full of antioxidants. The antioxidants,
again, can help reduce stress inside
blood vessels. Nutmeg also contains
important minerals, including magnesium,
potassium, and calcium. These minerals
work together to help control blood
pressure. The best way that I found to
use nutmeg is to sprinkle a small amount
in coffee, on fruit, or in oatmeal. So,
an important reminder that I really want
to hit home and emphasize. Spices only
help if you use them every day. Using
them every once in a while, even once a
week, likely will not change your blood
pressure. Small amounts used daily over
time will lead to lower blood pressure
numbers, and it's important to remember
that consistency beats perfection. Now,
you do not need to use all 11 spices at
once every single day. And here's a
simple plan that I found works best for
my patients. Use two or three spices per
meal and rotate them during the week. An
example day looks like for breakfast,
add cinnamon and ginger. For lunch, add
some garlic. And dinner, maybe add some
oregano. That's it. Simple food, small
steps, daily habits. You can also use
multiple spices that work well in
conjunction together, like the turmeric
and black pepper combinations. Basil and
oregano go really well together and you
can kind of mix and match. My last but
important piece of information is that
while spices may support in lowering
blood pressure, they don't replace
medical care. If you have blood pressure
consistently above 150 systolic at rest
or a diastolic above 90, kidney disease,
or heart disease and a prior smoking
history, you should always work with
your doctor. Spices are supportive tools
not an emergency treatment. If you found
this video helpful and want a simple
step-by-step plan to lower blood
pressure naturally up to 30 points in
just 90 days, I put everything together
in my blood pressure reset guide and you
can check it out using the link in the
description. Now, eating these spices
consistently can help bring down blood
pressure over time, but if you truly
want to make a lasting impact in your
blood pressure journey, they're best
used in conjunction with the top five
supplements known to lower blood
pressure naturally and I actually did a
